clue.text: Run off without a morsel? That's a minor inconvenience

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: to run off is to flee
a morsel is a bit

explanation.surface: Someone flees without having eaten anything, which is shrugged off as no great hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: FLEE goes round A BIT to give FLEABITE.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect's bite is the standard image of a trivial irritation, so the word is used figuratively for any small annoyance.

clue.text: A tailless donkey in a frenzy

indicators.note: an animal without its tail has lost its rear end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: taken as written
moke is British slang for a donkey

explanation.surface: A donkey with no tail charging about wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: MOKE, a British slang word for a donkey, loses its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to rush about wildly out of control, so the adverb matches being frenzied.

clue.text: Girl with bible brought up as a servant

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing something up reads it from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a lass is a girl
AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: A girl raised with the Bible to be a household servant.
explanation.walkthrough: LASS plus AV gives LASSAV, which read upwards spells VASSAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A vassal was a feudal subordinate owing service to a lord, and the word extends to any servant or underling.

clue.text: Number like every other number ringed by pen

indicators.note: something ringed is enclosed on all sides, so these letters go inside the other word

blocks.note: a pen for pigs is a sty
alternate whole numbers are even

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a number that resembles every second number and is enclosed by a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: Pen looks like a writing tool; here it is an enclosure for pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventy is a cardinal figure, ten times seven, so it is simply a number.

clue.text: Not one of the branches offering leading product

blocks.note: first meaning: the trunk railway route rather than a branch line
second meaning: a company's principal range of goods

explanation.surface: A firm's head office, not a branch, offering its flagship product.
explanation.definitionFit: Railways distinguish trunk routes from branch lines, and businesses speak of a principal range of goods as their core line.

clue.text: Real Madrid's darting moves with two wings

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase standing for a winged creature

indicators.note: quick darting moves shift things about, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the football club's name, letter for letter

explanation.surface: The football club's quick passing and its two wide players on the flanks.
explanation.walkthrough: Wings looks like football wingers; it is the insect's wings. A red admiral is a common butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: A red admiral is a butterfly, an insect with a pair of forewings and hindwings, loosely described as two-winged.

clue.text: Pile of muck in centre of lair

blocks.note: mid means the middle of
an animal's lair is its den

explanation.surface: Filth heaped up in the middle of an animal's lair.
explanation.definitionFit: A midden is a dunghill or refuse heap, the old word for a dump of dung and household waste.

clue.text: Pastry containing meat for picnic

indicators.note: one thing containing another holds it inside

blocks.note: a cake is a pastry
lamb is a meat

explanation.surface: A meat pie packed for an outdoor meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Pastry looks like the definition, but the answer is an American beach feast; the pastry is just the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A clambake is a seaside party where shellfish are cooked outdoors, an American beach picnic.

clue.text: A female or a male author

indicators.note: or offers an alternative, here an alternative arrangement of the letters that follow

blocks.note: taken as written
the author of a clue refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a writer is a woman or a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is only implied by or; A MALE with I for the setter rearranges into the woman's name AMELIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia is a girl's given name, so it can stand for a female person in crossword style.

clue.text: Corrupt captain, say

blocks.note: first meaning: foul, rotten
second meaning: a captain is an example of a military grade

explanation.surface: An accusation that a captain is crooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank can mean rotten or foul-smelling, and captain is one example of a grade in the armed forces.

clue.text: To back the result of a martinet matron?

definitions.text: the result of a martinet matron
definitions.note: a cryptic second reading, a noun phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: towards the rear of a ship

blocks.clueFragment: the result of a martinet matron
blocks.note: second meaning: a strict matron would make her hospital wards severe

explanation.surface: Wondering whether to support the consequences of a strict hospital matron.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as STERN WARDS: a martinet matron makes the wards stern.
explanation.definitionFit: Sternwards means towards the stern, the rear of a vessel, so it means moving backwards.

clue.text: Flashy money rarely half spent

indicators.note: when half of something is spent it is used up and gone, so only half the letters stay

blocks.note: tin is old slang for money
seldom means rarely

explanation.surface: Showy money that is hardly ever half used.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinsel as an adjective describes something showy but cheap, glittering without real value.

clue.text: Winter vehicle currently parking in Berkshire town

indicators.note: the earlier pieces go inside the place named afterwards

blocks.note: Slough is a town in Berkshire, west of London
currently means now
P is the abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A vehicle that is now parked in a town in Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowplough clears roads after snowfalls, so it is a machine used in the cold season.

clue.text: An African despot's held in the B compound

indicators.note: something held in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: taken as written
an means one, the Roman numeral I
Idi Amin, the Ugandan dictator

explanation.surface: An African dictator is detained in a compound.
explanation.walkthrough: Compound looks like a walled enclosure; it is a chemical. An stands for one, written as the numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: Thiamine is vitamin B1, one of the B group of chemical substances the body needs.

clue.text: Bravery shown by the lady is held in honour

indicators.note: one item held in another sits inside it

blocks.note: her refers to a lady
the Order of Merit, a British honour
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's courage is held in high regard.
explanation.walkthrough: The Order of Merit is an honour awarded personally by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroism is the quality of a hero, great courage in the face of danger.

clue.text: Goon allowed to have a bit of grass

blocks.note: Spike Milligan of the Goon Show, a British radio comedy
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A fool is permitted a little cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: Goon looks like an idiot and grass like cannabis; the Goon is Spike Milligan and the grass is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A spikelet is the small flower cluster that forms the basic unit of a grass head, so it is part of the plant.

clue.text: Richard about to drop a brick from crane

indicators.note: about means around, so one name surrounds the other piece

blocks.note: Dick is a short form of Richard
to drop a brick is a British idiom for making a blunder

explanation.surface: Richard is about to let a brick fall from a crane.
explanation.walkthrough: About to looks like going to; about is the container and to belongs to the idiom that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A derrick is a type of lifting machine with a jib, used to hoist heavy loads like a crane.

clue.text: Convict gets outside a prison? It's very hard

indicators.note: getting outside something means wrapping round it

blocks.note: a con is a convict
taken as written
stir is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A convict escapes outside a prison and finds life tough.
explanation.walkthrough: Stir is old British slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast iron is a brittle but rigid metal, so as an adjective it describes something firm and unyielding.

clue.text: Really excellent performance based on a very poor score

blocks.note: def is slang for excellent
an act is a performance
a zero score, nothing

explanation.surface: A truly excellent performance built on a dreadful score.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, based on puts O at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: De facto is Latin for in fact, describing what actually exists rather than what is official.

clue.text: Fruit punch included black stuff

indicators.note: one piece included by another sits inside it

blocks.note: a grape is a fruit
to punch is to hit

explanation.surface: A fruit punch that had something dark mixed in.
explanation.walkthrough: Fruit punch looks like a drink; it is a fruit and a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Graphite is the soft dark form of carbon used in pencil leads, so it is a black substance.

clue.text: You may see a hunchback, perhaps, double

blocks.note: first meaning: a bell-..., like Quasimodo, the hunchback of Notre-Dame
second meaning: a dead ..., a lookalike

explanation.surface: Seeing double, perhaps two hunchbacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Quasimodo rang the bells of Notre-Dame, and a ringer is also a close lookalike, as in dead ringer.

clue.text: Bother created by digger on the street

blocks.note: a mole is a burrowing animal
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Trouble caused by a digging machine on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: To molest originally meant to annoy or pester, so it shares the sense of troubling someone.

clue.text: Adult companion taken round biblical site

indicators.note: something taken round another encircles it

blocks.note: a mate is a companion
Ur of the Chaldees, Abraham's city in Genesis

explanation.surface: A grown-up friend is shown around a place from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur of the Chaldees is named in Genesis as Abraham's home city.
explanation.definitionFit: Mature means fully grown, the state of a grown-up person rather than a child.

clue.text: I learnt not to become self-opinionated

indicators.note: these words turn into something new, a rearranged form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A confession of having learnt not to be conceited.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone intolerant refuses to accept others' views, which is close to being opinionated and bigoted.

clue.text: Cold joint for a bit of food

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
the hip is a joint

explanation.surface: A cold joint of meat to nibble.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint looks like a roast; it is the body's hip.
explanation.definitionFit: A chip is a small piece or fried potato strip, a morsel to eat.

clue.text: Muscular contraction curtailed runner

indicators.note: curtailed means cut short, so the tail end goes

blocks.note: a cramp is a painful muscle spasm

explanation.surface: An athlete's race cut short by a muscle spasm.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Cram was a British middle-distance champion of the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Cram held world records at the mile and 1500 metres, so he is a famous athlete.

clue.text: Group working together in the distance

blocks.note: first meaning: an alliance or association
second meaning: an old measure of about three miles

explanation.surface: A team cooperating far away.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is an alliance of parties, and also an old unit of length of roughly three miles.

clue.text: Herb in paper covering's behind the salt

indicators.note: behind says the paper-and-covering pieces come after the sailor, so the order is swapped from the clue

blocks.note: a salt and a tar are both old words for a sailor
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
on means covering, lying on top of

explanation.surface: A herb wrapped in paper comes after the salt in the recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: Salt looks like the seasoning; it is a sailor, and behind sets the paper pieces after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarragon is an aromatic plant whose leaves are used in cooking, especially in French dishes.
